title: Audio-Vision: Sound on Screen (trans. C. Gorbman; 2nd ed. 2019 with foreword by W. Murch)
key_findings: 'Added value': the expressive and informative value a sound adds to an image, so that the information seems to come from the image itself.
'Synchresis': the spontaneous, irresistible weld between a sound and a visual event heard and seen at the same time, independent of logic (fight-scene punches).
Sound also 'temporally animates' and 'vectorises' an image (gives it direction toward an expected end).
practical_applications: Any sound placed exactly on a visual event will be read as that event's sound - basis of foley/cartoon SFX and of 'impossible' sounds for drawn characters.
limitations: Film-theory text (tier A as scholarly monograph) but its claims are analytical, not experimental. Read via secondary sources (Basanta 2017, reviews).

title: Shades of Synchresis
key_findings: Quotes Chion 1994: synchresis is 'the spontaneous and irresistible weld' (p.63); strength depends on meaning, context, gestalt and rhythm (pp.63-64); added value (p.5, p.21); vectorisation (pp.13-14).
Notes Chion's frameworks lack a measure of synchresis strength; the author's typology is not empirically tested.
practical_applications: Page-referenced Chion quotes for our docs.
limitations: Artist-researcher essay in eContact! 19.2; informal observations.

title: Interactions in perceived quality of auditory-visual displays
authors: Storms, Russell L.; Zyda, Michael J.
key_findings: 108 participants, 3 automated experiments manipulating pixel resolution / visual noise and audio sampling rate / audio noise.
High-quality audio with high-quality visuals raised perceived VISUAL quality vs visual-only baseline; low-quality audio with high-quality visuals lowered perceived audio quality.
With low-quality visuals, high-quality audio raised perceived audio quality.
practical_applications: Clean, full-band audio makes the same picture look better - spend effort on VO cleanliness and SFX quality, especially for AI/cartoon visuals.
limitations: Presence 9(6) 557-580; 2000-era displays; static image of a radio + music; small effects, lab setting.

title: The influence of video quality on perceived audio quality and vice versa
authors: Beerends, J. G.; de Caluwe, F. E.
key_findings: Video quality contributes significantly to judged audio quality; the video effect on audio judgements was larger than audio's effect on video judgements.
Video quality dominates overall audiovisual quality in non-conversational material.
practical_applications: Balance the Storms & Zyda result: audio helps perceived quality, but a bad picture cannot be rescued by sound.
limitations: JAES 47(5) 355-362; abstract only; sample details unverified.

title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.1359-1: Relative timing of sound and vision for broadcasting
key_findings: Subjective tests (Japan, Switzerland, Australia; NTSC and PAL) give detectability thresholds of about +45 ms to -125 ms and acceptability thresholds of about +90 ms to -185 ms on average (positive = sound advanced/early relative to vision).
Recommends overall sound/picture timing tolerance not exceeding +90 ms or -185 ms; final source selection to transmitter input within +22.5 ms / -30 ms.
Annex cites ITU-R BR.265: film sound/picture location within +/- half a frame (about +/-22 ms at 24 fps); the asymmetric tolerance means viewers are more sensitive to sound arriving early than late.
practical_applications: At 30 fps one frame = 33 ms: a hit SFX may sit 0-1 frame early but never more than ~1 frame early; up to ~3 frames late is still undetectable.
limitations: Broadcast lip-sync context (TV chains), not short-form social video; ITU-R page lists BT.1359-1 (11/98) as 'In force' (checked 2026-11-25).

title: Sound alters visual motion perception
authors: Sekuler, R.; Sekuler, A. B.; Lau, R.
key_findings: Two discs moving through each other look like 'streaming'; a brief click at the moment of overlap makes most observers see them 'bounce'.
practical_applications: A single well-timed contact sound changes what the eye sees happen - cheapest way to make cartoon contacts read.
limitations: Nature 385:308; read via abstract-level summaries; effect weaker in older observers (later work).

title: What you see is what you hear (sound-induced flash illusion)
authors: Shams, L.; Kamitani, Y.; Shimojo, S.
key_findings: Abstract: auditory information can qualitatively alter perception of an unambiguous visual stimulus, creating a striking visual illusion - overturning the view that vision always dominates.
Detail from secondary summaries (not in the abstract): a single flash with two or more beeps is seen as multiple flashes.
practical_applications: Rapid SFX can 'multiply' perceived visual events (sparkles, blinks, flickers) - use with care, it can also feel busy.
limitations: Nature 408:788 (2000); abstract read, full letter paywalled.

title: The construct of the multisensory temporal binding window and its dysregulation in developmental disabilities
authors: Wallace, M. T.; Stevenson, R. A.
key_findings: Review: the multisensory temporal binding window (TBW) is the epoch within which stimuli from different senses are likely to be bound; even at delays of a hundred ms or more, subjects still report audio-visual pairs as simultaneous on a high percentage of trials.

Points of subjective simultaneity typically fall in the visual-leading range; TBW size is highly variable between people, but left (auditory-leading) and right (visual-leading) windows correlate within a person.
TBW width depends on stimulus: narrowest for simple flashes/beeps, widest for speech; it recalibrates to environmental statistics and can be substantially narrowed by feedback training.
TBW is altered (wider) in autism, dyslexia and schizophrenia.
practical_applications: Explains why slightly late SFX still fuse but early SFX feel wrong; individual viewers differ.
limitations: Review centred on clinical populations; window widths vary by task (SJ2, SJ3, TOJ). Read via PMC4326640 (Neuropsychologia 64:105-123).

title: The International Affective Digitized Sounds (IADS-2): affective ratings of sounds and instruction manual
authors: Bradley, M. M.; Lang, P. J.
key_findings: Standardised set of 111 everyday sounds rated on valence, arousal and dominance (Self-Assessment Manikin); IADS-1 1999, IADS-2 2007; uneven coverage of valence-arousal space.
practical_applications: Evidence that everyday sounds (screams, laughter, erotic sounds, alarms, birds) carry stable affect - basis of our emotion -> sound table.
limitations: Technical report not read; facts from papers that use IADS (e.g. Stevenson & James 2008).

title: Affective auditory stimuli: characterization of the International Affective Digitized Sounds (IADS) by discrete emotional categories
authors: Stevenson, R. A.; James, T. W.
key_findings: Collected discrete-emotion ratings for the IADS, a database of 111 sounds already rated on valence, arousal and dominance, so sounds can be chosen under both dimensional and categorical theories of affect.
practical_applications: Pick SFX by the discrete emotion they reliably evoke, not by name only.
limitations: Abstract read on Springer page (Behavior Research Methods 40(1):315-321); per-category numbers not read. IADS-E (2018) expands the set.

title: Perceptual bias for rising tones
key_findings: Listeners reliably overestimated the change in level of rising-level tones relative to equivalent falling tones; the bias was stronger at higher levels.
Author proposes a selective advantage (rising intensity can signal an approaching source) and an asymmetry in neural coding of harmonic dynamic intensity change.
From earlier secondary search (not re-checked): replicated in rhesus monkeys (Ghazanfar et al. 2002); a 2026 paper proposes a 'speed prior' explanation.
practical_applications: Risers / crescendos feel bigger and nearer than their dB change; downlifters feel like release - use risers sparingly or they over-promise.
limitations: Nature 395:123-124; abstract read via RePEc; the adaptive explanation is the author's interpretation.

title: The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Craft monograph by a Hollywood foley artist: spotting, cueing, footsteps, props, cloth, sync; one of the first scholarly books on foley.
practical_applications: Foley layers: feet, cloth/moves, specifics (props) - our sfxlib follows the same split.
limitations: Publisher page only; craft knowledge (tier D).

title: Dense Clarity - Clear Density (Transom, 2005)
key_findings: Murch places sounds on a conceptual spectrum from 'Encoded' (clearest example: speech, meaning carried by a code) to 'Embodied' (clearest example: music, sound experienced directly); most sound effects lie between.

'Law of Two-and-a-Half' (first noticed on THX-1138 robot footsteps, 1969-70): within one 'colour' of sound an audience can follow about two-and-a-half layers; at three they congeal into one new 'many' (robots walking in a group); two simultaneous conversations can just be followed, three cannot.

If layers are spread evenly across the spectrum, about five layers per 'moment' (he suggests any five-second section) is the maximum that keeps the mix both dense and clear: one dialogue, one music, one 'linguistic' effect (footsteps), one 'musical' effect (atmospheric tonality), one balanced effect.
Worked out on the Apocalypse Now premixes, where too many good sounds together 'melted into an unimpressive racket'.
practical_applications: Limit simultaneous layers of the same kind; spread layers across the encoded-embodied spectrum (VO + one music + one SFX family).
limitations: Practitioner essay (tier D): his own heuristic from experience, not an experiment; the left-right-brain explanation he offers is speculative.

title: Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema
key_findings: Practical and theoretical guide to dialogue, effects, music and ambience for storytelling and emotion; frequently cited by music-psychology papers as one of few sources on combined sound design.
practical_applications: Vocabulary for briefs (texture, rhythm, density, point of audition).
limitations: Bibliographic only; craft.

title: [exact title not confirmed] Kock & Louven 2019 empirical study on sound design and music in moving pictures
key_findings: States that neither music psychology, film psychology nor neuroscience has profoundly explored the power of sound design scientifically.
practical_applications: Honest framing: most sound-design rules are craft, not science.
limitations: Seen only as a search snippet.

title: Hitchcock flicks give your brain tunnel vision (report on Bezdek et al. fMRI study of suspense)
key_findings: Report (2015) on Bezdek et al. (Neuroscience): participants in fMRI watched 10 suspense film clips (3 Hitchcock, plus e.g. Alien) while flashing checkerboards stimulated the visual periphery; in high-suspense moments activity in peripheral parts of the calcarine sulcus dropped and central-field activity rose - attention narrowed to the centre.
The changes were not explained by moment-to-moment visual features (e.g. brightness) but by plot and threat; suspense was rated by a separate group with a slider.
Effects of sound and music were explicitly left untested (Zacks: 'think of Jaws').
practical_applications: Suspense focuses the eye - put the key object in the centre during sound-built tension and silence.
limitations: Science journalism; primary paper not read. fMRI measure, not behavioural probes - the earlier entry wrongly said 'slower responses, missed peripheral probes'.

title: [PhD thesis on silence in film sound] Kingston University
key_findings: Argues a general overview of the uses of silence is lacking in sound and film studies.
practical_applications: Silence design is under-researched: treat our silence rules as craft.
limitations: Snippet only; title not confirmed.

title: Introduction to Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTF's): Representations of HRTF's in Time, Frequency, and Space (invited tutorial)
authors: Cheng, C. I.; Wakefield, G. H.
key_findings: Duplex theory (Rayleigh): azimuth from interaural time differences (ITD) and interaural intensity differences (IID); above about 1500 Hz ITD becomes ambiguous (wavelength comparable to head size) and head shadow makes IID the useful cue.

Duplex theory alone leaves a 'cone of confusion' (Hornbostel & Wertheimer 1920), most acute in the median plane where ITD and IID are about zero; HRTF spectral colouring by torso, head and pinna resolves elevation and front/back.
Elevation cues are thought to depend on the pinna, with frequencies near 6-8 kHz important; Blauert: median-plane localisation needs broadband sound.
Measured HRTFs can synthesise spatial sound over headphones.
practical_applications: Phones/earbuds: stereo panning = ILD only; real 3D needs binaural (HRTF) rendering and is lost on a phone speaker.
limitations: Authors at University of Michigan (copy hosted on a University of Maryland lab site); tutorial from about 1999-2001, so newer HRTF personalisation work is not covered; venue not printed on the copy read.

title: Sonic logos: can sound influence willingness to pay?
authors: Krishnan, V.; Kellaris, J. J.; Aurand, T. W.
key_findings: Lab experiment: the number of tones in a sonic logo influenced willingness-to-pay non-linearly.
practical_applications: A short repeated sound signature (motif) carries brand meaning; keep it simple and consistent.
limitations: Journal of Product & Brand Management; snippet only.

title: The impact of the sonic logo's acoustic features on orienting responses, emotions and brand personality transmission
key_findings: Psychophysiology + self-report lab experiment linking sonic-logo acoustic features to orienting response, emotion and perceived brand personality.
practical_applications: Acoustic features of a motif (tempo, pitch contour, timbre) shape the personality the brand seems to have.
limitations: Snippet only; findings not detailed.
